Minnows beating whales

 

As investors survey the damage from the Jensen Huang scandal, equal-weight index investing is having its day in the sun.

 

The most widely held S&P 500 index funds are weighted by market capitalization, so the megacap companies account for the biggest chunks. That has meant growing concentration risk for everyday index investors, leaving them vulnerable if a single giant stumbles—like Nvidia losing more than $1.8 trillion in market value in just over a month.

 

When the year started, the 10 biggest companies made up just over 40% of the S&P 500, more than doubling since a decade earlier. Today they’re just under 40%. S&P 500 funds, created on the promise of broad diversification, are now megaweight tech funds.

 

For years, however, the obvious solution had been worse than the problem. Equal-weighted funds chronically trailed their market-cap-weighted counterparts.

 

Over the last decade, the equal-weighted S&P 500 more than tripled, while the main index more than quadrupled. Quarterly rebalancing means equal-weight funds sell winners and buy losers to reset each stock to 0.2% of the fund. Until recently that was a recipe for what famed fund manager Peter Lynch called “diworsification,” trimming winners too early and missing large gains.

 

Now the script has flipped. The past few weeks—marked by midterm elections and the Nvidia sex-and-espionage scandal—offer a quintessential example of the risks equal weighting is designed to hedge against.

 

As of Oct. 28, right before the scandal broke, the S&P 500 Equal Weight Index was up 15.0% year-to-date, slightly ahead of the main index’s 14.2% return. Since then, the gap has blown open. Equal-weight is up 17.0% year-to-date compared with 11.5% for the regular index (and 19.8% versus 13.6% over the past 12 months).

 

Equal-weighted Russell 1000 and Nasdaq-100 indexes also have bested their traditional counterparts over both stretches.

 

A big reason for the most recent outperformance: Nvidia’s stock has fallen 24% since Oct. 28. That has dragged down the S&P 500 yet barely dented the equal-weight version. Notably, Nvidia didn’t pull down every other megacap tech stock with it, either.

 

Apple, Amazon.com and Meta Platforms all gained during that stretch. Competing chip makers like Broadcom, Advanced Micro Devices and Micron dropped after Election Day, when Democrats won new majorities in Congress. They then surged last week as Nvidia announced an internal investigation and Huang resigned as chief executive.

 

The rotation benefited equal-weight funds, where flyweights and megaweights start each quarter on the same footing.

 

None of this means megaweight index investing is over, or that equal-weight strategies will keep outperforming. Equal-weight funds typically have higher expense ratios—about 0.20 percentage point compared with as little as 0.03 point for traditional S&P 500 funds. But lately they’ve been well worth the cost.

 

Sometimes it pays to be a worrywart.
